**Yes, such a subset exists.**

**Construction.** Let
$$S = \{(n,\, n^2) : n \in \mathbb{Z}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2.$$

**No three collinear points.** The set $S$ lies on the parabola $y = x^2$. Any (non-vertical) line $\ell: y = mx + b$ meets this parabola where $x^2 = mx + b$, i.e. where $x^2 - mx - b = 0$, a quadratic equation with at most **two** real solutions. A vertical line $x = c$ meets the parabola in exactly one point. Hence every line in the plane intersects the parabola $y = x^2$ in at most two points, and therefore intersects $S$ in at most two points. In particular, **no three points of $S$ are collinear**.

**No area.** The set $S$ is countable (it is indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$). Every countable subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ has two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero: each point is a set of measure zero, and a countable union of measure-zero sets has measure zero. Equivalently, $S$ can be covered by countably many disks of arbitrarily small total area (cover the $n$-th point by a disk of radius $\varepsilon/2^{|n|+1}$). Thus $S$ has **no area**.

**Conclusion.** The set $S = \{(n, n^2) : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is a subset of the plane that simultaneously has no area (measure zero) and contains no three collinear points. Therefore such a subset **is constructible**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
